To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) endogenous progenitor cells in the adult CNS show a reduced neurogenic potential compared to their situation in vitro, (ii) astrocyte-derived signals and changes in the extracelluar matrix influence the differentiation of progenitor cells, and (iii) the extracellula matrix is a potential target for manipulation of the environment after brain injury to enhance stem cell therapy.
astrocytes in the injured CNS express neural progenitor markers, but do not give rise to neurons in large numbers, and that the ECM might play a role for the limited regeneration capacity.

the ECM composition in the injured CNS is not permissive for neuronal differentiation and that the interaction of the transplanted cells with the host ECM is crucial for the success of stem cell-based therapy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of the ECM on stem cells in the context of brain damage.
the interaction of endogenously activated cells with their microenvironment and the impact on the regenerative capacity after brain damage.
the interaction of endogeneous and transplanted cells with their environment after brain damage, with focus on the ECM.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is still much to be learned about the interaction of stem cells with the ECM in the damaged CNS.
the environment in the damaged CNS is not permissive for the generation of new neurons.
stem cells are not the limiting factor in the regenerative capacity of the adult CNS, but that the environment plays a crucial role.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
endogenous and transplants cells are influenced by signals in the damaged brain, and that these signals might be manipulated in a way to promote regeneration.

astrocytes in vivo have limited potential for neurogenesis, and that the ECM in the damaged CNS does not provide a supportive environment for neuronal differentiation of astrocytes and transplanted cells.
astrocytes in vivo do not behave as progenitor cells, but rather as a barrier that needs to be crossed by transplanted cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a better understanding of the interaction between stem cells and the environment is necessary to develop effective strategies to improve regeneration after brain damage.
the environment of the adult CNS is not optimal for the generation of new neurons.
the environment of the CNS plays a crucial role in the regulation of stem cells.
